benchmark_details.name: Library Cards
benchmark_details.overview: Tests models on extracting bibliographic data (author, title, year, place and the card's type) from typed, printed and handwritten cards of the University Library Basel's dissertation catalogue (before 1980).

purpose_and_intended_users.goal: Measure how well vision-language models turn catalogue cards of historical dissertations into structured bibliographic records (author, title, year, place, pages, publisher, format, shelfmark, subjects) and tell full descriptions apart from cross-reference cards. The results serve researchers and developers comparing models on historical document extraction, and practitioners in libraries, archives and digital humanities projects who choose a model for converting card catalogues into machine-readable metadata.
tasks: bibliographic field extraction from card images
classification of a card as a dissertation description or a cross-reference
purpose_and_intended_users.limitations:
The 263 cards are a random sample from a single catalogue (see Source), not stratified by period, language or card condition. They mix typed, printed and handwritten entries, mostly in German. Only 10 are cross-references, so results on that class rest on very few cases.

The ground truth was created by correcting GPT-4o output, so where the corrector accepted an ambiguous reading it may lean towards that model's choices. It follows the normalisation conventions described under Annotation, so it measures agreement with those conventions rather than with a neutral cataloguing standard. It contains at least one error: `00575005` has year `0`.

All fields weigh equally, so a wrong shelfmark costs as much as a wrong author. The match threshold (see Calculation) is strict for short fields: `X, 184` against `X,184` or `Thieme Verlag` against `Thieme` scores as wrong. Fields empty on both sides are not counted, so a sparse card has a small denominator and a single error moves its F1 considerably.
out_of_scope_uses: evaluating full-text transcription of catalogue cards
evaluating extraction of the thesis defence, faculty, supervisor or later editions, which the cards sometimes record but the schema does not
drawing conclusions about the authors named on the cards

data.source: Catalogue cards of the *Dissertationenkatalog bis 1980*, the dissertation catalogue of the University Library Basel (Universitätsbibliothek Basel), https://ub.unibas.ch/cmsdata/spezialkataloge/ipac/searchform.php?KatalogID=ak2. The benchmark uses a random sample of the cards for the roughly 700,000 dissertations the library collected before 1980. The dissertations come mainly from Switzerland and neighbouring countries. A card describes one dissertation, usually its author and the published version of record, sometimes also the defence or other published versions, without separating these explicitly. Some cards are cross-references: they name an author followed by `s.` (German *siehe*, "see") on a separate line and point to another card.
data.format:
One JPG per card, about 1000×600 px and 75 KB, typed, printed or handwritten. Each card has one ground-truth JSON file; two further files, `00604370.json` and `00604375.json`, have no image and are never scored. In a ground-truth file, `provider`, `model`, `test_time`, `execution_time` and `scores` record how the draft was produced; only `response_text` is scored. It follows the `Document` dataclass in `dataclass.py`:

```json
{
  "type": {"type": "Dissertation or thesis"},
  "author": {"last_name": "Müller", "first_name": "Maurice Edmond"},
  "publication": {
    "title": "Die hüftnahen Femurosteotomien unter Berücksichtigung der Form,Funktion und Beanspruchung des Hüftgelenkes",
    "year": 1957,
    "place": "Stuttgart",
    "pages": "X,184",
    "publisher": "Thieme",
    "format": "4'"
  },
  "library_reference": {"shelfmark": "AT Zürich 7", "subjects": ""}
}
```

- `type.type`: `Dissertation or thesis` or `Reference`
- `author`: `last_name`, `first_name`
- `publication`: `title`, `year`, `place`, `pages`, `publisher`, `format`; the dataclass also allows `editor`, which no ground-truth file fills
- `library_reference`: `shelfmark` (often beginning `Diss.` or `AT`, or marked `Standort:`), `subjects`

The ground truth stores `year` as an integer in 258 files and as a string in 5. The response schema allows a string or null, and the local Pydantic validator converts a numeric year to a string. The scorer compares both as strings, so `1957` and `"1957"` match.
data.annotation: GPT-4o drafted the ground truth; Gabriel Müller and Maximilian Hindermann corrected it by hand with the `ground_truther.py` tool. They followed the extraction rules of [prompt.txt](prompts/prompt.txt): a card with `s.` on its own line is a `Reference`, and pages are given without `S.`. In addition, pages keep unnumbered parts (`IV S. + 67-74 S.` becomes `IV 67-74`), and the octavo mark is kept exactly as on the card (`8°` or `8'`).
data.collection_date: Source documents: dissertations published 1593–1979, most of them 1880–1979. Added to the benchmark: April 2025.
data.contamination_controls: None. The card images, prompts and ground truth have been public in this repository since April 2025.

methods: zero-shot structured extraction from a single card image per request
structured JSON output requested using the `Document` dataclass

two prompt variants: [prompt.txt](prompts/prompt.txt) (127 tests) asks for `year` as an integer, although the response schema allows only a string or null, which can make constrained decoding emit whitespace until the output cap; [prompt_year-string.txt](prompts/prompt_year-string.txt) (4 tests, the default for new tests) asks for a string and is otherwise identical. Scores of the two variants are not directly comparable for a model affected by the loop
output cap: the repository default of 16,384 tokens per request, adjusted per model in `scripts/benchmark_base.py`
methodology.calculation:
Every terminal field of the JSON (for example `publication.title`) present in the response or the ground truth is compared; empty strings count as missing. Legacy `examination` fields, `publication.reprint_note` and `library_reference.publication_number` are excluded. Field values are compared with a rapidfuzz similarity score (`ratio`/100; values are compared as strings), and a field is a match at a score of 0.92 or above.

- TP: both have a value and the score is at least 0.92
- FP and FN: both have a value but the score is below 0.92 (the field counts once as each)
- FP: only the response has a value
- FN: only the ground truth has a value
- neither: both are empty

F1 macro averages the per-card F1, each rounded to two decimals. F1 micro sums TP, FP and FN over all cards before computing F1. A response that is not parseable JSON is left out of both rather than scored as zero.

For example, for the ground truth above and a response that differs only in `first_name` (`Maurice`), `pages` (`X, 184`) and `publisher` (`Thieme Verlag`), the card has 7 TP, 3 FP and 3 FN (`subjects` is empty in both and not counted), so precision, recall and F1 are 0.70.
methodology.interpretation: Scores range from 0 to 1; higher is better. F1 macro weights every card equally; F1 micro weights cards by their number of filled fields, so full descriptions count more than sparse cards and cross-references. A score does not separate misreadings from differences in normalisation (see Limitations).
methodology.baseline_results:
Model results are available on the [benchmark page](https://rise-services.rise.unibas.ch/benchmarks/p/benchmarks/library_cards) and in `results/<date>/<test_id>/` at the repository root. Compare runs with the same prompt, scoring rules and ground-truth revision, and report the number of successfully scored objects alongside the score. No fixed baseline run is designated.

Observed across models: models generally do well on clearly typed cards with standard layouts and worse on handwritten cards and those with non-standard layouts or abbreviations. Common errors are omitted or misparsed shelfmarks and subject classifications, small formatting differences in pages and publisher, publisher names with an added "Verlag", and variant notations of format and academic abbreviations.
methodology.validation: The annotators checked the ground truth by hand against the images. Scoring is deterministic; the scorer is covered by the repository's test suite. No inter-annotator agreement was measured.
methodology.validity_justification: Field-level F1 reflects the downstream use: each field becomes a value in a catalogue record, so a field is either usable or needs correction.

ethical_and_legal_considerations.privacy_and_anonymity: The cards name the authors of dissertations together with the title, place and year of the work; the same data is in the library's public catalogue. The cards are not anonymised: they hold metadata of published works and no personal data beyond the authorship the publications themselves state.
ethical_and_legal_considerations.compliance_with_regulations: The cards are bibliographic records of published works, so no personal-rights issue arises. The University Library Basel provided the card images and granted their use under CC0; no licence is published with the catalogue itself. No separate reuse terms are stated for the ground truth. No ethical review was carried out.
